title: The annual review is broken
text:
Every December, in offices around the world, a curious ritual takes place. Managers and employees sit down together, often reluctantly, to discuss the previous twelve months. Forms are filled in, numbers from one to five are assigned, and both parties leave the room feeling vaguely dissatisfied. It is called the annual performance review, and it is time we admitted that it does not work.

Consider, first, the timing. Asking a manager to evaluate someone's work over an entire year is asking them to perform a feat of memory that few humans are capable of. Research on so-called recency bias shows that evaluators give disproportionate weight to the most recent weeks. An employee who had a brilliant spring and a difficult November will be judged largely on November. Feedback that arrives months after the event is also of little practical use: by the time you hear that your presentation in March was poorly structured, you have already given five more.

Then there are the ratings. Reducing a year of complex, collaborative work to a single number is not merely crude; it is actively harmful. Studies suggest that when people receive a rating, they focus almost entirely on the number and barely listen to the explanation that follows. Those rated as "average" – the majority, by design – frequently leave the meeting demotivated, even if their manager's comments were overwhelmingly positive. Worse still, ratings are often linked to bonuses, which turns what should be a developmental conversation into a negotiation over money.

Defenders of the system argue that organisations need some formal way of making decisions about pay and promotion, and that without a structured process, favouritism would flourish. This is a fair point. But it does not follow that the annual review, in its current form, is the best way of achieving those aims. Several large companies have abandoned ratings altogether in favour of frequent, informal check-ins, and the evidence so far suggests that performance has not suffered. In some cases, employee engagement has risen noticeably.

What would a better system look like? It would separate conversations about development from decisions about pay. It would replace a single annual meeting with short, regular discussions – monthly, perhaps, or after each major project. It would encourage feedback from colleagues, not just from managers. And it would focus on the future rather than the past: not "how did you do?" but "what do you need to do better?"

None of this is revolutionary. Good managers already do much of it instinctively. The problem is that the formal system often works against them, demanding paperwork and numbers when what people actually need is honest, timely conversation. It is not that we need to measure people less carefully. We need to stop pretending that a form filled in once a year is the same thing as paying attention.
